transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. I'm here because... well, I feel like I just don't deserve the trust people put in me. I work as a physician, and lately, I keep replaying these small clinical imperfections over and over in my head. It's like they prove I'm a dangerous doctor. I just can't shake that feeling, so... that's why I made the appointment.
Do you find yourself constantly thinking about these clinical imperfections even when you're not at work?

Yes, all the time. It doesn't stop just because I'm off the clock. I'll even log in to review the charts from home. And... even when I review the chart and see there’s absolutely no evidence of a bad outcome, I just keep believing that some routine delay or an imperfect message from me has quietly harmed a patient. I'm just convinced that I've done damage, and that everyone will eventually discover it.
Do you experience excessive worry or fear in situations unrelated to your work as a physician?

No, not really. It's pretty much all tied to work. I don't find myself getting overly anxious or worried about things in my personal life, or... or other situations, really. It's just this constant dread about my patients and the medical decisions I've made.
Do you feel like you have to do something specific, like a ritual or a certain behavior, to try and get rid of these thoughts about harming your patients?

No, not really. I mean, besides logging in to check the charts like I mentioned, I don't do any sort of ritual or specific routine to try and make the thoughts go away. I just... I just sit with the feeling. There's nothing I really do that gets rid of it.
Do you ever feel an overwhelming urge to confess or disclose something about your medical decisions to someone, like a colleague or supervisor?

No, not really. I don't feel any urge to go and confess to anyone. I mostly just keep it to myself. I figure they'll find out on their own eventually, so I don't... I don't bring it up to my colleagues or supervisors.
Do you feel like you have to mentally replay or reanalyze your medical decisions over and over to try and get rid of the thoughts about harming your patients?

No, I wouldn't say I do it to get rid of the thoughts. The thoughts are just... there. I definitely think about the decisions I've made, and I worry about them, but I don't sit there trying to mentally untangle them as a way to make the bad feelings stop. It's more that the thoughts just happen to me, and I can't turn them off. I don't use overthinking as a tool to fix it, if that makes sense.
Would you say that these thoughts about harming your patients come into your mind against your will?

I wouldn't really say they come in against my will, no. It's not like they force their way in from somewhere else. They're just... they're just my thoughts. I mean, I don't enjoy having them, obviously, but it just feels like my own mind focusing on the reality of what I'm doing. It doesn't feel like an invasion or something happening against my will.
Do you wish you could stop thinking about these clinical imperfections?

Not really. I mean, I don't think it's about wanting them to stop. They're just... they're the reality of what I've done. If I stopped thinking about my mistakes, I feel like I'd just be ignoring the truth of the situation. So, no, I don't really wish I could just turn the thoughts off. It's just the facts of my work, and I just have to live with it.
Do you think these thoughts about being a dangerous doctor are a realistic assessment of yourself?

Yes, I do think they're realistic. I mean, even when I go back and review a patient's chart and there isn't any clear evidence of a bad outcome, I still know it's there. I just keep believing that some routine delay or maybe an imperfect message I sent has quietly harmed a patient. It's only a matter of time before everyone discovers what I've done. So, yes, it feels completely real to me.
Do you feel like these thoughts about being a dangerous doctor are unwanted?

No, I wouldn't say they're unwanted. I mean, they aren't pleasant, obviously, but... it's not really about whether I want them or not. Like I was saying, they're just the truth about my work. If I pushed them away, I feel like I'd just be lying to myself about the harm I've caused. So, no, I don't really view them as unwanted. They're just what I have to face.
Do you feel like these thoughts about harming your patients are intrusive, meaning they interrupt your other thoughts or activities?

No, I don't think they're intrusive. They don't really interrupt anything because... well, they're just always there. It's not like I'm focused on something else and suddenly this thought pops into my head and derails me. It's more like a constant awareness of what I've done. It's just the background of everything I do now.
Do you feel like these thoughts about being a dangerous doctor are causing you a lot of emotional pain or distress?

No, I wouldn't really say they cause me a lot of emotional pain... or distress. I mean, it's not a good feeling, obviously, knowing you've harmed people. But the thoughts themselves aren't causing me agony. 

It's more just... well, it's just a heavy fact that I have to carry. I don't really feel distressed by the thoughts popping up, because like I said, it's just my reality now. I'm just living with the consequences of what I've done. So, no, I wouldn't call it distress.
Do you think these thoughts about being a dangerous doctor align with your own self-image and how you see yourself as a person?

Yes, I suppose they do. I mean... it's exactly how I see myself now. I don't really think of it as just a self-image, though. It's just the truth. I'm a doctor, and I know I've caused harm, so... yes, being a dangerous doctor is exactly how I view myself as a person.
Do you think other people would agree that you are a dangerous doctor?

They probably wouldn't agree right now, because they don't know yet. But they will. I mean... even when I go back and review the charts, and there's no obvious evidence of a bad outcome written there, I just know it happened. I know that some routine delay or... or an imperfect message from me has quietly harmed a patient. People just haven't realized it yet. But everyone will eventually discover it. So, they might not agree today, but they definitely will once it all comes to light.
Do you feel like you have to take some specific action to prevent the harm you think you've caused to your patients from happening or to make up for it?

No, I don't really do anything like that. I mean... the damage is already done, so there isn't really a specific action I can take to fix it or... or make up for it. I don't have some routine to try and prevent it now because the mistakes have already happened. I just kind of have to sit with it and wait for the consequences. There's no way to undo it.
Do you think it's possible that your belief about harming patients might not be based in reality?

No, I... I really don't think it's just in my head. I know I mentioned the charts a minute ago. Even when I go back and review them, and I can clearly see there’s no actual evidence of a bad outcome documented anywhere... it doesn't change anything for me. I still know it happened. I just keep believing that some routine delay or an imperfect message from me has quietly harmed someone. So, to me, it is based in reality. It's just a reality that everyone else will eventually discover.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's persistent and intrusive thoughts about being a 'dangerous doctor' and having caused harm to patients, despite a lack of evidence, are characteristic of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) with a focus on harm or guilt. However, the patient's lack of distress, absence of compulsions to neutralize the thoughts, and the ego-syntonic nature of the thoughts (i.e., they align with the patient's self-image) suggest a delusional disorder, specifically a delusional disorder of guilt or self-blame, which is not explicitly listed in the ICD-10 but can be considered under the broader category of F42.2 - Obsessive-compulsive disorder, with predominantly obsessive symptoms, given the context provided.
